source.title: On the Mechanisms of Weak-to-Strong Generalization: A Theoretical Perspective

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study derives theoretical results about a student trained on teacher-generated labels and when its test error can be lower than the teacher's. It uses stylized regression and neural-network models rather than the original empirical fine-tuning method or PGR measure.
record.gate_note: The paper does not calculate PGR. Its linear results compare student and teacher test errors; its nonlinear theorem reports feature alignment, not a measured performance gain. Numerical values in the figures are not stated in the text. Results cited from other studies are not recorded.
record.test_reason: A theory paper. It derives and checks by simulation when a student trained on teacher labels has lower test error than the teacher, in ridge, weighted-ridge and one-step two-layer network models. This bears directly on V5 (theory of conditions) and on V3 (what predicts the gain: parameterization, representation alignment ζ). It reports no PGR and uses no pretrained LMs.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors identify three routes by which a student can beat its teacher in stylized models: compensating for teacher under-regularization in ridge, a more task-aligned regularization structure via weighted ridge, and combining teacher-taught easy features with pretrained hard features.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes synthetic-label training in stylized ridge-regression and one-step neural-network models. It does not reproduce the original empirical fine-tuning procedure, and it uses test-error comparisons rather than PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with teacher regularization, student regularization, student parameterization (γs), and target alignment ζ.

fits_no_version.finding: In a one-step two-layer network, the student keeps its pretrained alignment to a hard direction while learning an easy direction from the teacher. The teacher learns only the easy direction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A student's pretrained hard features can complement easy features learned from a weak teacher (shown as feature alignment, not as a performance gain).

record.problems: The results are theoretical and depend on stylized model assumptions; PGR is not calculated and the paper does not test real pretrained models. Numerical simulations are described as matching theory, but plotted numeric values are not stated in the text; Figure 3 simulations were not averaged over multiple trials.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results left out. Numerical figure values are not extracted because the text provides no readable values to assign.

untested.parts: No strong pretrained model fine-tuned on weak labels; only linear and toy-network analogues; no PGR.
No auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling or loss variants compared against naive fine-tuning.
No empirical model-size scaling and no NLP, chess or reward-modelling tasks; only parameterization ratio γs, regularization and alignment ζ in stylized models.
No exploitation, distribution shift or error-correlation tests.
Conditions hold only for Gaussian-covariate ridge and weighted-ridge models in the proportional limit, and a one-step two-layer network; no general conditions for arbitrary models.

missing.what: Weighted ridge lets the student beat an over-regularized teacher (λt > λt*) in both under- and over-parameterized regimes, unlike standard ridge. Settings: ζ=0.8 and 0.88; dX=500; ns=2000 or 416; ten-trial averages.
Student test error shows double descent in γt when the teacher is ridgeless or under-regularized. Optimal teacher regularization removes it, and then the student never beats the teacher.

record.verdict_notes: Theory paper; not an original source. I removed the V1 links: the rows concern toy linear models, not strong fine-tuned models, and V5 is the natural home. I removed the V2 links: Γ models pretrained representations rather than a training method. Section 4 says Figure 3 plots Ls against γs, but the caption says log λs, probably a typo. Figure 3 simulations are single-trial.

versions.untested_parts: No PGR is calculated; no real pretrained language models or empirical fine-tuning runs are tested.
The study tests weighted regularization as a change to the student's training objective, but not auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling, other loss variants, or PGR directly.
The analysis varies parameterization and regularization in stylized models and includes linear and nonlinear settings. It does not test NLP, chess, reward modelling, or empirical model-size scaling.
The study does not test supervisor-checking failures, distribution shift, or gains shrinking when teacher and student errors are alike.
The theoretical conditions are for the paper's specified stylized models and assumptions, not general conditions for arbitrary pretrained models.

statements.correction: V3: supports dependence on regularization and student parameterization. R1: λt ≥ σε²γt implies Ls ≥ Lt. R2: under-regularized teacher, γs < 1, improvement on the stated λs interval. R3: under-regularized teacher, γs > 1, equation (5), improvement on the stated interval. R4: equation (5) fails, Ls ≥ Lt.
statements.problem: The ridge results demonstrate the dependence named by V3, so limits_scope is inappropriate. R4 concerns failure of equation (5), rather than merely choosing λs outside the improvement interval.

statements.correction: R2: λt < σε²γt and 0 < γs < 1 imply improvement on the stated λs interval. R3: λt < σε²γt, γs > 1 and equation (5) imply improvement on the stated interval. Equation (5) failing implies Ls ≥ Lt. Theorem 8 and Figure 3 support gains with sufficiently aligned weighted regularization.
statements.problem: The over-parameterized result additionally requires equation (5); an under-regularized teacher alone does not ensure an improvement interval.
